title.raw: Called to the Bharosa Cell or Women's Cell in Pune Over a 498A Complaint? What Happens at Each Stage
title.rendered: Called to the Bharosa Cell or Women’s Cell in Pune Over a 498A Complaint? What Happens at Each Stage

content.raw:
In short: In Pune, a wife's complaint of cruelty or dowry harassment is often referred to the Bharosa Cell or a women's cell for counselling before, or alongside, any police action. A call from the cell is not an arrest and not yet an FIR, but what happens there can shape whether an FIR follows. It is usually sensible to attend, carry your documents, stay factual and avoid signing anything under pressure. Arrest of the husband or relatives is not automatic: for an offence like Section 85 BNS (old 498A IPC), the law expects a notice-first approach, and anticipatory bail is a decision to take on the specific risks in your case.

Many husbands first hear of a complaint through a phone call asking them to come to the cell, often soon after a divorce or maintenance case is filed. The fears are always the same: will I or my parents be arrested, and should I even go? This guide walks through each stage.

Complaint, counselling, FIR: the usual sequence in Pune

The Bharosa Cell is the Pune Police counselling and support cell for women and families. Matrimonial complaints are commonly referred there, or to a women's cell attached to the police, so that both sides can be heard and counselling attempted before or alongside police action. The exact practice can differ from case to case and over time, so treat the sequence below as typical rather than fixed.

  1. Complaint: The wife gives a written application to the police, the women's cell or the Bharosa Cell.
  2. Call or notice to attend: The husband, and sometimes his family, are asked to attend on a date.
  3. Counselling sessions: Counsellors or officers hear both sides, sometimes over more than one sitting. The aim is reconciliation or an agreed separation.
  4. Outcome: The complaint may be closed if the parties settle, or the matter may be sent to the police station, where an FIR may be registered.

The Supreme Court has recognised that in matrimonial disputes the police may make a preliminary inquiry before registering an FIR (Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh, 2013). Counselling at the cell fits within that space.

The offence itself. Cruelty to a married woman by her husband or his relatives, formerly Section 498A IPC, is now Section 85 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), with Section 86 BNS defining "cruelty". The punishment is imprisonment up to three years and fine. Complaints frequently add the Dowry Prohibition Act, criminal breach of trust over streedhan (Section 316 BNS, old 406 IPC), or hurt and threats, depending on the allegations.

StageWhat it means for youSensible step
Call from the cellNo FIR yet, no arrestNote the date, officer and case reference; collect documents
CounsellingBoth sides are heard; settlement may be exploredAttend, stay calm and factual, sign nothing you do not understand
Matter sent to police stationAn FIR may be registeredGet legal advice on arrest risk and anticipatory bail
FIR registeredInvestigation begins; notice under Section 35 BNSS is the usual routeRespond to notices; keep records of every visit

Should you attend? What to carry and what not to say

Attendance at counselling is not the same as answering a court summons, but ignoring the cell usually removes the chance to be heard early and can make it more likely that the complaint moves straight to an FIR. For most people, attending after taking advice is the safer course.

What to carry:

  • Marriage certificate and photographs of the wedding, if relevant.
  • Copies of any divorce, maintenance or domestic violence petitions and notices.
  • Messages, emails and call records relevant to the allegations, kept in their original form.
  • A list of streedhan and gifts and their present location, if that is an issue.
  • Proof of where you and your relatives live, particularly for family members who never lived with the couple.
  • A short written chronology of the marriage.

What not to do:

  • Do not lose your temper, make allegations you cannot support, or contact your wife outside the process in a way that can be called a threat.
  • Do not sign settlement terms, undertakings or admissions under pressure. Ask for time to read and take advice.
  • Do not hand over original documents; give copies.
  • Do not post about the dispute on social media.

Arrest risk for husband and relatives

This is usually the main worry, so it is worth being precise.

  • Notice first, not arrest first: In Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014), the Supreme Court held that police should not arrest automatically in 498A cases and must follow the notice-of-appearance procedure for offences punishable with up to seven years. Under the new law that procedure is in Section 35 BNSS (old Sections 41 and 41A CrPC). Section 85 BNS carries a maximum of three years, so it falls within this protection.
  • Relatives: The Supreme Court has repeatedly cautioned against roping in the husband's relatives on general, vague allegations with no specific role. This is a safeguard, not immunity. Where a relative is accused of specific acts, the police can still act.
  • Cooling-off and family welfare committees: Courts have at different times suggested a cooling-off period or a family welfare committee before coercive action in 498A cases. The position has changed over the years, and how it applies in a particular police station today should be checked with your advocate rather than assumed.

A notice under Section 35 BNSS asks you to appear and cooperate. If you comply with the notice, arrest generally requires recorded reasons. See police notice under Section 35 BNSS for how to respond.

When anticipatory bail makes sense

Anticipatory bail is not needed in every 498A complaint. It becomes more relevant where the risk of arrest is higher, for example:

  • The complaint alleges injuries, or more serious sections are added (such as attempt to murder or dowry death allegations).
  • The police have indicated an intention to arrest, or the notice procedure is not being followed.
  • Family members are elderly or unwell, or a member lives abroad and needs to travel.
  • There are parallel cases that suggest the dispute is escalating.

Anticipatory bail is sought under Section 482 BNSS (old Section 438 CrPC), usually first before the Sessions Court in Pune and, if refused, before the Bombay High Court in Mumbai. Read more on anticipatory bail and on what to do once a 498A FIR is filed.

Settlement, mediation and quashing

Many matrimonial disputes end in a negotiated settlement: return of streedhan, a lump-sum payment, mutual consent divorce and withdrawal of cases. Points to keep in mind:

  • Put every term in writing, including which cases will be withdrawn or quashed and in what order.
  • Link payments to steps, such as recording statements in the mutual consent divorce.
  • Cruelty under Section 85 BNS is generally not compoundable, so the parties cannot simply withdraw it. Once an FIR or chargesheet exists, a settled case is usually closed by asking the Bombay High Court to quash it under its inherent powers, now Section 528 BNSS (old Section 482 CrPC).

Quashing can also be sought where the allegations, even if taken as true, do not disclose an offence, or are vague against particular relatives. See FIR quashing.

Illegal demands

No one is lawfully entitled to demand money from you to "close" a complaint or avoid arrest, and no officer can demand cash as a condition of not arresting you. If anyone does:

  • Do not pay.
  • Write down the date, time, place and name or designation of the person, and keep any messages.
  • You may report it to senior police officers or to the Anti-Corruption Bureau; your advocate can help you decide the right route.

Bail conditions, such as sureties, are set by a court in a written order, not by negotiation at the police station.

For broader information on matrimonial criminal cases, see 498A and domestic violence defence. If you have been called to the cell, discussing your papers with an advocate before the first sitting can help you prepare.

Frequently asked questions

Is attending the Bharosa Cell mandatory?

Counselling is a pre-FIR process, not a court summons. However, not attending usually means losing the chance to present your side early, and the complaint may then be forwarded for registration of an FIR. In most cases it is advisable to attend, after taking legal advice on what to carry and say.

Will my parents and sisters be arrested?

There is no automatic arrest and no blanket immunity. Section 85 BNS carries up to three years, so the notice-first procedure under Section 35 BNSS applies, and courts have cautioned against acting on vague allegations against relatives. The real risk depends on what is specifically alleged against each person.

Can I take a lawyer to counselling?

Practice varies. Some sittings are meant for the parties alone, while in others an advocate may be allowed to accompany. Even where counsel cannot sit in, an advocate can prepare you beforehand and review any document before you sign it.

Do I need anticipatory bail before counselling?

Not always. A call to counselling is not an FIR. Anticipatory bail is usually considered when an FIR is likely or registered and there are added risk factors, such as serious sections, injury allegations, a clear intention to arrest, or family members who must travel.

What if the complaint was filed after I filed for divorce?

The timing can be a relevant fact, and it should be recorded in your chronology with copies of the divorce papers. It does not by itself end the complaint; the police and courts look at the specific allegations.

Note: This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Every case turns on its own facts, and the law and court practice can change. Please consult a qualified advocate about your situation.
